reference.title: Twin Strangers
reference.text: Twin Strangers is an online project that helps people find a stranger who looks just like them. It was set up by Niamh Geaney from Dublin and two friends.

reference.title: Glossary
reference.text: Erasmus scholarships — a programme which allows students from the European Union to study in another country.

tasks.instruction: Look at the photos. One of them is of identical twins, but two of them are of complete strangers. Read about the project Twin Strangers. Which photo is of twins?
tasks.note: SB 1a–b (угадать → проверить по тексту) → Blank с вариантами в hint
tasks.context:
Two women recently met by chance at Bremen University, in Germany. One was English, and one was Irish, and they were both on Erasmus scholarships. Nothing unusual there, except for one thing. The two girls look identical. Their hair is the same colour and length, they’re the same age and size, and when you see them together, in the photo they put on social media, you would think that they were identical twins. In fact, Cordelia Roberts and Ciara Murphy are unrelated.
It seems that it is not uncommon for people who are unrelated to look almost identical. Niamh Geaney, from Dublin, and two friends were so interested in trying to find their ‘twins’ that they set up an online project called Twin Strangers. Very quickly, Niamh found a remarkably similar-looking stranger who lived just a few miles away. It’s perhaps not so surprising, as both young women look typically Irish, with dark hair and very pale skin, but then Niamh found another lookalike – Luisa Guizzardi, who is from Genoa in Italy!

reference.title: So / Neither + auxiliary + I
rows: I love classical music. / I don’t like classical music.
So do I. / Neither do I.
I went to a concert last night. / I didn’t like the film.
So did I. / Neither did I.
I wouldn’t like to go there.

reference.text: We use So… I / Neither… I to say that we have something in common with somebody. So + auxiliary + I responds to positive sentences; Neither + auxiliary + I responds to negative sentences. The auxiliary depends on the tense of the verb that the other speaker uses. We can also use Nor instead of Neither: Nor did I. Neither is usually pronounced /ˈnaɪðə/, but also /ˈniːðə/.

reference.wrong: So I do. / Neither I do.
reference.right: So do I. / Neither do I.
reference.why: Word order: So / Neither + auxiliary + I.

tasks.context: In the USA, identical twin brothers were adopted soon after they were born. One brother was adopted by a couple named Lewis in Lima, Ohio, and his brother was adopted by a couple named Springer in Dayton, Ohio. By coincidence, both boys were called ‘Jim’ by their new parents. Jim Springer’s parents told him that he had an identical twin brother, but that he was dead. But Jim Lewis knew the truth. For many years he did nothing about it, but when he was 39, he decided to try to find his brother. Six weeks later, the two Jims met for the first time in a café in Dayton, and they probably had a conversation something like this…
